1226.title: The Transitus (3 October 1226)
1226.hook: Francis dies lying on the bare ground singing Psalm 141
1226.howItsDone: Franciscans and some parishes keep a Transitus service on the eve of Saint Francis's feast, retelling his death with readings, Psalm 141 and his Canticle of the Creatures, often by candlelight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace prayer, honestly: not his words, but his shape. Your line was francis-shaped.

Evening, at the little church of Saint Mary of the Angels below Assisi. Francis is dying, and he knows it. His brothers crowd around. He's blind or nearly, worn out, and the early lives say he carries wounds in his hands and side. He asks for something strange: take off my habit, and lay me on the bare ground. No bed, no pillow. Just the earth he called sister and mother. Then, the old biographers say, he began to sing. Today, the night Francis died, and the name his brothers gave it.
screen: `EVENING, AT SAINT MARY OF THE ANGELS.` → `LAY ME ON THE BARE GROUND.` → `AND HE BEGAN TO SING.`

segments.voice: Franciscans call that night the Transitus, Latin for a passing over. Not an ending, a crossing. The word echoes the Gospel Francis asked to hear that evening, John chapter thirteen, which opens in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass out of this world to the Father." Francis wanted to die the way his Lord had passed: poor, stripped, among friends. The early lives tell it in pieces. He blesses the brothers around him. In Saint Bonaventure's telling, he says he has done his part; may Christ teach them theirs. Then he sings Psalm one hundred forty-one, as numbered in the Latin Bible the friars prayed: "I cried to the Lord with my voice." Near the end it asks: "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name." A dying man asking to be let out, and calling it praise. Earlier, Francis had added a last verse to his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for our Sister Bodily Death, whom no one living can escape. Celano tells that when death came near, Francis greeted it as family: welcome, my sister death. The man who called the sun brother called death sister too. Bonaventure adds a quiet detail: larks, birds of daylight, gathered over the roof at dusk and sang. Sign or lovely story, the brothers remembered it. And if death feels close or wanted for you tonight, please don't carry that alone: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
screen: `TRANSITUS: A PASSING OVER.` · `JOHN 13: HIS HOUR WAS COME.` · `PSALM 141, SUNG ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `DEATH, GREETED AS A SISTER.` · then, large: `BRING MY SOUL OUT OF PRISON.`

segments.voice: Lie flat if you can, on the floor or a bed, arms loose, or lean back and let your body be heavy, and feel the ground holding you up. If you pray, say the line Francis sang, I cried to the Lord with my voice, and rest, then the other: bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name; if not, just notice how it feels to be held, with nothing to do.
The Transitus. Francis's passing over: dying on the bare ground, singing a psalm, greeting death as his sister. Today's word.
Your line: welcome, sister death. For Francis, even the last night was a crossing, met among friends. Go gently tonight.

1227.title: Franciscans today
1227.hook: friars in cities, soup kitchens and missions
1227.howItsDone: Franciscan friars and sisters serve in parishes, soup kitchens, shelters, schools, hospitals and missions, and Catholics often support their works with gifts of money, food or time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transitus: Francis on the bare ground, singing a psalm, greeting death as family. Your line was welcome, sister death.

Before sunrise in a big city, a line is already forming outside a side door: men with backpacks, a mother with a stroller, an old man in a coat too heavy for the weather. The door opens, and the person holding it is a friar. Down the street, another hears confessions in a downtown church at lunchtime. Across an ocean, another teaches in a village school, or sits with the sick in a clinic. Francis died on the bare ground in Assisi. His brothers never stopped walking. Today, where you might find them now.
screen: `A LINE BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `A FRIAR HOLDS THE DOOR.` →`HIS BROTHERS NEVER STOPPED.`

segments.voice: Francis didn't found a monastery on a hilltop. He sent his brothers out. His Rule pictures them going through the world owning nothing, working with their hands, taking what they need as poor men do. So the friars ended up where people are, in towns, then cities, and that's still the shape. The family of Francis now has several branches of friars, among them the Friars Minor, the Conventuals, and the Capuchins from a few days ago. There are the Poor Clares behind their grilles, praying for the world. There are Franciscan sisters running schools and hospitals. And there are lay Franciscans, married people with jobs and kids, who follow Francis in ordinary life. What do they do? Ordinary things, close to the poor: a soup kitchen, a shelter, a parish on a block nobody else wanted, a chaplain in a prison or hospital, a mission far from home. Jesus's words in Matthew could hang over the door, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in." One more thing. Francis is often said to have told people to preach the Gospel always and use words only if necessary. The early sources don't record him saying it. What his early Rule does say is close: all the brothers should preach by their deeds. The friar at that side door is doing just that.

Choose one small gift you could give, a few dollars, a bag of groceries, an hour, or simply finding out where it is; if you pray, pray for the people in that line and the people holding the door.

1228.title: A Franciscan day at home
1228.hook: simplicity, praise for creation, joy with the poor
1228.howItsDone: Lay Franciscans and other Catholics drawn to Francis keep a simple rule of life at home: grace before meals, a short daily prayer such as morning or evening psalms, a simpler way of living, and regular service with the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Franciscans today: friars, sisters and lay followers at soup kitchens and missions. Your line was still walking.

Give Francis your kitchen for a day, and here's what might change. He wouldn't bring luggage. He'd thank God for the bread before he ate it, and probably for the salt too. He'd stop at the window to greet the weather by name. He'd ask who on your street is hungry, and want to sit with them, not just send something over. By evening the house might feel lighter, not because anything was cleaned, but because less was needed. Three weeks with Francis end today, not in Assisi, but at home.
screen: `FRANCIS MOVES IN FOR A DAY.` → `NO LUGGAGE. THANKS FOR THE SALT.` → `A LIGHTER HOUSE BY EVENING.`

segments.voice: A Franciscan day at home has three threads, and you've met them all. The first is simplicity. Francis heard the Gospel tell the apostles to take nothing for the road, and took it literally. At home that doesn't mean selling the couch. It means asking, one thing at a time: do I need this, or does it need me? Jesus points to the flowers in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin." The second thread is praise. The whole Canticle is a list of reasons to thank God: sun, wind, water, fire, earth. A Franciscan home turns small things into praise: grace before meals, a psalm in the morning, thanks at the window. The third is joy with the poor, not pity from a distance. Francis wrote that when he went among the lepers, what had seemed bitter was turned into sweetness. In his Admonitions he ties having little to gladness: where there is poverty with joy, he says, there is no greed and no grasping. The three hold each other up. Simplicity without praise turns grim. Praise without the poor turns comfortable. Joy with the poor, without simplicity, runs out of room at the table. Franciscans have a short greeting for all of it, which some still write at the end of their letters: peace and good.
screen: `SIMPLICITY: DO I NEED THIS?` · `PRAISE: TURN SMALL THINGS INTO THANKS.` · `JOY WITH THE POOR, NOT PITY.` · `THREE THREADS HOLD EACH OTHER UP.` · then, large: `CONSIDER THE LILIES OF THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Look around the room and pick one thing you could do without today, the second coffee, the scroll before bed, the purchase in your cart, and let it go, just for today. Then pick one small thing to praise, the light through the window, the chair holding you, and thank God for it by name if you pray, or just say thank you into the room; last, hold one person with less than you for a breath.
A Franciscan day at home. Simplicity, praise for creation and joy with the poor, woven together in an ordinary house. Today's word.

1229.title: The innkeeper (1203)
1229.hook: Dominic stays up all night talking with an innkeeper who held other beliefs
1229.howItsDone: Dominicans tell the story of the innkeeper as the seed of their order, and Dominican friars and sisters still give much of their lives to study, preaching and long conversations with people who hold other views.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Franciscan day at home, and the end of three weeks with Francis. Your line was praise and simplicity.

An inn in Toulouse, in the south of France. It's late. Two travelers from Spain come in off the road: a bishop named Diego, on an errand for his king, and a priest of his cathedral, a Castilian named Dominic. They're tired. They want a bed. But Dominic gets talking with the man who runs the inn, and finds his host holds beliefs very different from his own. He could nod politely and go upstairs. He doesn't. Today, the conversation that, by tradition, started an order.
screen: `AN INN IN TOULOUSE, LATE.` → `TWO TRAVELERS FROM SPAIN.` → `DOMINIC DOESN'T GO UPSTAIRS.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Jordan of Saxony, who followed Dominic as head of his order and wrote down how it began. The innkeeper, Jordan says, belonged to the movement the Church called heresy and historians call the Cathars. They taught that the material world was not the good work of a good God, and they lived lives of hard self-denial that impressed their neighbors. So Dominic, in Jordan's telling, spent the whole night with his host, talking earnestly and warmly. Not shouting him down, not threatening: talking, listening, and talking again, until dawn. By morning, Jordan says, the man could not resist the wisdom and spirit of what he heard, and returned to the Catholic faith. Notice what the story chooses to remember. Not a crowd, not a church council. One man, one table, one long night. A line from the first letter of Peter fits. In the Douay-Rheims it asks believers to be "ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." The next verse says how: with modesty and fear. Tradition says that night planted something in Dominic. Before it, he was a canon praying in his cathedral's choir. After it, he wanted to spend his life explaining, patiently, to people who saw the world another way. That's what his order would be called: the Preachers.

1230.title: Preaching poor
1230.hook: Dominic's answer to heresy was to live poor and preach well; later Dominicans also served the Inquisition
1230.howItsDone: Dominican friars take vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and give themselves to study and preaching; Dominicans and other Catholics also speak openly today about the order's part in the Inquisition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the innkeeper, and Dominic at his table in Toulouse until dawn. Your line was all night talking.

The pope's envoys rode through the south of France the way important churchmen traveled: good horses, servants, baggage. They'd been sent to win people back from the Cathars, and it wasn't working. People listened to the envoys, then looked at the Cathar preachers, who went on foot and lived plainly, and compared. The envoys were ready to give up. Then they met two travelers from Spain, a bishop named Diego and his companion Dominic, and Diego gave them advice they didn't want to hear. Today, that advice, and the harder history that came after it.
screen: `GOOD HORSES, SERVANTS, BAGGAGE.` →`IT WASN'T WORKING.` → `ADVICE THEY DIDN'T WANT.`

segments.voice: Diego's advice, as Jordan of Saxony records it, was blunt. Send the horses home. Go on foot. Carry no gold or silver. Live and preach as the apostles did, and let people see the Gospel before they hear it. It's what Jesus tells his disciples in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes." Diego didn't just say it. He sent his own household home and set out on foot, Dominic beside him. They begged their food, slept where they could, and argued patiently in town squares and at kitchen tables. That's the seed of what Dominic later founded: the Order of Preachers, friars who would be poor so they could preach well, and study hard so they could preach truly. Now the harder part, and this path holds it too. In the generations after Dominic, popes chose Dominican friars, along with Franciscans, to serve as inquisitors: judges in Church courts that tried people accused of heresy. Those courts used harsh methods, and some of the people they condemned were handed over to the civil authorities and put to death. That's part of the Dominican story, not a footnote to it. The Catholic Church has since asked God's forgiveness for violence used in the service of truth. Holding both means not choosing one memory: a bishop who sent his horses home, and the courts that came later, in the same habit. The order still carries both.

1231.title: The nuns first (Prouille, 1206)
1231.hook: Dominic's first community was of women
1231.howItsDone: Dominican nuns live enclosed lives of prayer, study and work in monasteries, praying especially for the preaching of the friars; Dominicans honor Prouille as the first house of their family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, preaching poor: horses sent home, and the harder memory of the courts that came later. Your line was poor preachers.

Ask who the first Dominicans were, and you may picture men: friars in white and black, walking to the cities, preaching in the squares. But go back to the south of France, to a small place called Prouille, at the foot of a hill. Before there was an Order of Preachers, before the pope had approved anything, Dominic and his bishop Diego gathered a household there. Not of preachers. Of women. They prayed, they worked, they lived together behind walls. Today, the community that came before the friars.
screen: `FRIARS IN WHITE AND BLACK?` → `A SMALL PLACE CALLED PROUILLE.` → `NOT PREACHERS. WOMEN.`

segments.voice: Why women? The reason is in Jordan of Saxony's account. In that region, he says, some families who were noble but poor had handed their daughters to the Cathars to be raised and taught, because they couldn't provide for them. When women like these came back to the Catholic faith, they had nowhere to go. So Diego and Dominic founded a monastery at Prouille to receive them. It became the first house of what grew into the Dominican family. The friars came after. That's an odd start for an order of preachers: its first community didn't preach in the streets at all. It prayed. Dominicans sometimes speak of their nuns' prayer as going before the friars' words. A preacher walking into a hostile town at dawn has someone already praying for him. And the Gospel has its own women who came first in their way. Luke tells how women traveled with Jesus and the Twelve: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and others, in the Douay-Rheims, "who ministered unto him of their substance." They paid for the road. Luke places them at the cross, and at the empty tomb. At Prouille too, women are the first chapter: before the order had a name, a rule or a pope's approval, it had a house of women praying.

1232.title: The order approved (1216)
1232.hook: approved at last, Dominic's few friars scatter to the university towns
1232.howItsDone: Dominican friars live in communities, often in cities and near universities, and preach, teach and serve as chaplains; they write O.P., for the Order of Preachers, after their names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prouille: before a house of preaching brothers, a house of praying women. Your line was the nuns came first.

A small group of men in Toulouse. They have a name now, the pope's approval, and a future together. The sensible move is to stay: build the house, grow slowly, side by side, under the eye of the man who gathered them. Instead, the early accounts say, Dominic tells them to split up. Some to Paris. Some to Bologna. Some back to Spain. The brothers object: too few, too new, they hardly know the work yet. He sends them anyway. Today, the order approved, and the first thing it did with its approval: scatter.
screen: `A NAME, AND THE POPE'S APPROVAL.` → `THE SENSIBLE MOVE: STAY.` → `DOMINIC SAYS: SPLIT UP.`

segments.voice: On paper the approval is quiet: the bishop of Rome signs, and a band of preachers from the south of France becomes an order of the whole Church. Their name says the job: the Order of Preachers. Named not for a place or a house, but for a task, and a task like that pulls you outward. Near its end, Mark's Gospel has Jesus sending his followers out. In the Douay-Rheims: "Go ye into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Dominic seems to have taken that at its word. A saying credited to him, in substance: grain heaped up in a barn goes bad; grain scattered on a field bears fruit. So the brothers went where the people were, to the cities: markets, workshops, crowds of strangers. And in some cities, something newer still, the universities, full of young men arguing about everything. The friars went straight in. They studied there, preached there, and found new brothers there, as students and teachers asked for the habit. That choice shaped the whole order. The Rule of Saint Benedict asks a monk to promise stability, to stay with one community. A friar's life was built for the road. And the approval didn't make Dominic careful. He had very few brothers, and he gave them away.
